title: Bytes in memory order
description:
A 32-bit number takes four bytes. On a PC they are stored **little-endian**: lowest byte first.

Write two functions.

- `toBytes(value)` returns the four bytes of `value` in the order they would sit in memory. `toBytes(0x12345678)` is `{ 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12 }`.
- `fromBytes(bytes)` does the reverse and returns the number those four bytes make.

Use shifts and masks, the operations from the lesson, so that your code would give the same answer on any processor. `memcpy` and `reinterpret_cast` are not allowed here.
hints: `value & 0xFF` keeps the lowest eight bits and clears the rest. That is the byte that goes first in memory.
`value >> 8` shifts everything right by eight bits, so the second-lowest byte becomes the lowest. Do "take the lowest byte, then shift" four times.
Going the other way, start with the **last** byte, which is the highest. For each byte: shift the value left by eight to make room, then combine the byte in with `|`.
`bytes[i]` is a `std::uint8_t`. Storing the result of `value & 0xFF` in it needs `static_cast<std::uint8_t>(...)`, because the expression is a wider type.
rules: Use shifts and masks so the answer does not depend on the processor.
